info.title: Knee MRI - Fine Spacing Corpus
info.subtitle: CoAtNet fine-tuned for the 12 knee findings on the Fine Spacing slice sampling.
info.description:
![Dread Development — Johnathan Wagner](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/dread-orbit-web.webp)

[![Kaggle](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/kaggle-bar.png)](https://www.kaggle.com/dreaddevelopment) [![GitHub](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/github-bar.png)](https://github.com/Bojackdidit) [![Website](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/website-bar.png)](https://dreaddevelopment.com) [![Email](https://bojackdidit.github.io/dread-cinematic-banner/buttons/email-bar.png)](mailto:john@dreaddevelopment.com)

CoAtNet 384 weights for scoring twelve findings on a knee MRI study. They score 0.932 on the public leaderboard as a single model, with no ensembling, read at 78 windows per study.

The corpus behind them samples 80 slices per study across 2 to 98 percent of each series, cropped to a 140 mm box using the DICOM pixel spacing and resized to 336 pixels. The eighty slots are filled with 22 slices from a sagittal fluid sensitive series, 18 from a second sagittal series, 15 from a coronal fluid sensitive series, 10 from a second coronal series and 15 from an axial series. Scoring uses 78 windows per study, which is every window position an 80 slice volume holds.

This is the finest sampling in the set, 1.20 percent of the stack per slice. It came from separating span from spacing. Spreading 44 slices across the same 2 to 98 percent span thins the sampling to 2.18 percent per slice and scored 0.917, below the 0.926 it started from, while 64 slices across that span restores the density and scored 0.928. Widening the span only pays if slices are added to keep the sampling dense, and carrying that further is what produced this corpus.

A NOTE ON THE SCORES

Every number quoted across this family of datasets goes with a window count, and the two are not separable. The same weights read differently depending on how much of each study is scored:

44 slices at 42 windows, 0.926
64 slices at 42 windows, 0.924, and the identical weights at 62 windows, 0.927
64 slices over the wide span at 62 windows, 0.928
80 slices at 78 windows, 0.932

So a checkpoint from this set scored on a 64 slot volume at 62 windows is not getting the geometry it was trained on, and the 0.932 will not be there. When comparing checkpoints, hold the window count fixed, otherwise two things are moving at once.

HOW TO USE IT

The checkpoint is a PyTorch dict, not a bare state dict, saved with torch.save. Keys: model (the weights), arch (the timm backbone name), res (the input size the model expects) and lab (the twelve finding names in the order the model outputs them). Load it with torch.load(path, map_location='cpu', weights_only=False), build the backbone from ck['arch'], attach the twelve-way attention pooling head, then load ck['model'].

A working end-to-end inference notebook, including the preprocessing these weights expect, is here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/dreaddevelopment/knee-mri-twelve-findings-from-a-single-model

WHAT THE MODEL DOES

Three neighbouring slices are stacked into the three channels of one image, so the network sees a little of what lies above and below the middle slice. Each of these three-slice windows goes through the backbone, and the windows are pooled by an attention layer with separate weights for each of the twelve findings, so each finding can draw on the slices that actually show it.

The twelve findings, in the order the model outputs them, are ACL tear, MCL tear, medial and lateral meniscus tears, osteoarthritis in the medial, lateral and patellofemoral compartments, joint effusion, synovitis, a Baker's cyst, bone contusion and fracture.

Trained on report-distilled soft labels (rsna-knee-labels) over the preprocessed slice stacks (knee-raptor-corpus and knee-raptor-corpus-ext). One of a family of slice sampling variants meant to be ensembled, so pair it with the wide span and wide dense checkpoints for a diversity boost.
